Problem 1 (a)

```{r}
#Problem_1_a_Simulation function

#' Move the particle one step
#'
#' @param location A numeric vector of length 2 containing
#'   according to the output, the current x and y coordinates.
#' @param movement A direction code: 1 = right, -1 = left,
#'   2 = up, and -2 = down.
#'
#' @returns A numeric vector of length 2 containing
#'   the updated x and y coordinates.

walk <- function(location, movement) {
  if (length(location) != 2 || !is.numeric(location)) {
    stop("error")
  } else {
    if (movement == 1) {
      location <- location + c(1, 0)
    } else if (movement == -1) {
      location <- location + c(-1, 0)
    } else if (movement == -2) {
      location <- location + c(0, -1)
    } else if (movement == 2) {
      location <- location + c(0, 1)
    } else {
      stop("error")
    }

    #return(location)
  }
}

#' Simulate n steps starting from the origin (0, 0).
#' At each step after the first, keep the previous direction
#' with probability p; otherwise, randomly select one of
#' the four directions.
#'
#' @param n A positive integer specifying the number of steps.
#' @param p A number between 0 and 1 specifying the probability
#'   of keeping the previous direction instead of resampling.
#'
#' @returns A numeric vector of length 2 containing the final
#'   x and y coordinates.

momentum_walk <- function(n, p) {
  if (n < 1 || n %% 1 != 0 || p < 0 || p > 1|| !is.numeric(n)||!is.numeric(p) ) {
    stop("error")
  } else {
    location <- c(0, 0)
    movement <- sample(c(-2, -1, 1, 2), size = 1)

    #cat("step 1\n")
    location <- walk(location, movement)
    #print(location)

    if (n > 1) {
      for (i in 2:n) {
        #cat("step", i, "\n")

        if (runif(1) < p) {
          location <- walk(location, movement)
        } else {
          movement <- sample(c(-2, -1, 1, 2), size = 1)
          location <- walk(location, movement)
        }

        #print(location)
      }
    }

    return(location)
  }
}
momentum_walk(10, 0.6)
```

```{r}
#' Simulate a momentum random walk using sapply
#'
#' Simulate n steps starting from the origin (0, 0).
#' Use sapply to process the remaining steps after the first.
#' At each step, keep the previous direction with probability p;
#' otherwise, randomly select one of the four directions.
#'
#' @param n A positive integer specifying the number of steps.
#' @param p A number between 0 and 1 specifying the probability
#'   of keeping the previous direction instead of resampling.
#'
#' @returns A numeric vector of length 2 containing the final
#'   x and y coordinates.

momentum_walk2 <- function(n, p) {
  if (n < 1 || n %% 1 != 0 || p < 0 || p > 1|| !is.numeric(n)||!is.numeric(p) ) {
    stop("error")
  } else {
    location <- c(0, 0)
    movement <- sample(c(-2, -1, 1, 2), size = 1)
    location <- walk(location, movement)
  if (n > 1) {
      sapply(2:n, function(i) {

        if (runif(1) >= p) {
          movement <<- sample(c(-2, -1, 1, 2), size = 1)
        }

        location <<- walk(location, movement)
        return(location)
      })
    }

    return(location)
  }
}
momentum_walk2(10, 0.6)
momentum_walk2(1000, 0.6)
```

```{r}
#I used set.seed() to solve this question. I used seed 1 for n = 10 and seed 2 for n = 1000, with p = 0.6 in both cases. Resetting the same seed generates the same sequence of pseudorandom numbers, so repeating the same function with the same inputs produces identical final coordinates.
set.seed(1)
momentum_walk(10,0.6)

set.seed(1)
momentum_walk(10,0.6)

set.seed(2)
momentum_walk(1000,0.6)

set.seed(2)
momentum_walk(1000,0.6)
```

Problem 1 (e)

```{r}
#Problem 1_(e) Monte Carlo simulation

# The five momentum probabilities.
p_values <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)

# (i) Simulate 1000 walks for each p and save their final distances.
distances <- sapply(p_values, function(p) {
  replicate(1000, {
    location <- momentum_walk(1000, p)
    sqrt(location[1]^2 + location[2]^2)
  })
})

# (ii) Calculate the mean final distance for each p.
mean_distances <- colMeans(distances)

# (iii) the results in a table.
results <- data.frame(
  p = p_values,
  mean_distance = mean_distances
)

print(results)
#(iv) The mean final distance increases as p increases, rising from approximately 27.80 at p = 0 to 122.83 at p = 0.9. Higher momentum makes the walker more likely to continue in the same direction, allowing it to travel farther from the starting point on average.
```

```{r}
#The other four strongly right-skewed results: The count of most advertisements is relatively low, while the count of a few advertisements is very high. Therefore, I applied the log(1 + x) transformation to these four results to reduce skewness and compress large values. Adding 1 allows for including zero counts, as log(0) is undefined. The transformed results will be used for subsequent regression analysis.

# Transform the four right-skewed variables.
youtube_new$log_view_count <- log1p(youtube_new$view_count)
youtube_new$log_like_count <- log1p(youtube_new$like_count)
youtube_new$log_dislike_count <- log1p(youtube_new$dislike_count)
youtube_new$log_comment_count <- log1p(youtube_new$comment_count)

# Plot the transformed distributions.
hist(youtube_new$log_view_count,
     main = "Log-transformed view counts",
     xlab = "log(1 + view count)")

hist(youtube_new$log_like_count,
     main = "Log-transformed like counts",
     xlab = "log(1 + like count)")

hist(youtube_new$log_dislike_count,
     main = "Log-transformed dislike counts",

hist(youtube_new$log_comment_count,
```

```{r}
#problem 3_(c) Fitting linear regression models
#Now we do the linear regression model first consider view count

outcomes <- c(
  "log_view_count",
  "log_like_count",
  "log_dislike_count",
  "log_comment_count"
)

seven <- c(
  "funny",
  "show_product_quickly",
  "patriotic",
  "celebrity",
  "danger",
  "animals",
  "use_sex"
)

results <- data.frame()

# Fit 28 separate models, each adjusting for year.
for (outcome in outcomes) {
  for (seven in seven) {

    # Construct the regression formula.
    model_formula <- as.formula(
      paste(outcome, "~", seven, "+ year")
    )

    # Fit the model.
    fit <- lm(model_formula, data = youtube_new)

    # Extract the coefficient table.
    coef_table <- summary(fit)$coefficients

    # Store the characteristic's coefficient and p-value.
    results <- rbind(
      results,
      data.frame(
        outcome = outcome,
        seven=seven,
        estimate = coef_table[2, "Estimate"],
        p_value = coef_table[2, "Pr(>|t|)"]
      )
    )
  }
}

# Report the coefficient and p-value for all 28 models.
print(results, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
d_data <- youtube_new[
  complete.cases(
    youtube_new$log_view_count,
    youtube_new$danger,
    youtube_new$year
  ),
]

# Response variable
y <- d_data$log_view_count

# Construct the design matrix:
# intercept + danger + year
X <- cbind(
  1,
  d_data$danger,
  d_data$year
)

# Calculate beta_hat using the matrix formula
beta_hat <- solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X) %*% y

beta_hat


# Fit the same model using lm()
fit_d <- lm(
  log_view_count ~ danger + year,
  data = d_data
)

coef(fit_d)
```
